segments.description: Coaches, we introduce now Oscar Wagner, a trailblazer in modern tennis coaching and the creator of modern tennis methodology. With a coaching career spending over 50 years, Oscar has transformed how players and coaches approach the game. In his session, Modern Tennis, Rational Awareness vs. Linear Thought, he will share innovative strategies that challenge traditional methods and enhance player development. Welcome, Oscar. Tennis revolution, introduction. At the top level of the game, professional players keep revolutionizing tennis. They utilize rotational force that simplifies and strengthens their game both physically and in the way they affect the flight of the ball. Rotation is a fundamental principle of the physical universe. Rotation is present in every structure, from the smallest atom to the largest galaxies. In tennis, the use of topspin permits a player to hit harder than ever and still bring the ball down on the court. Balls that for their force and height seem to be on the way out, miraculously land inside the lines, putting pressure on their opponents. Unfortunately, though simple and easy to apply, teaching rotational principles correctly at the entry level is not sufficiently presented to the public, and this makes tennis a difficult sport to learn. Topspin, rotational forces do not apply only to the action of the stroke, but also to the ball's reaction to the impact.

Extreme ball rotation assists gravity in accelerating the ball downward and rebounding it higher. Topspin creates greater air resistance on the top of the ball than on the bottom, resulting in a more pronounced arcing trajectory. Extreme topspin actually creates more pressure on the top of the ball, pulling it downward and making it bounce back even further, the Magnus effect. The remaining rotation further challenges the opponent when he makes contact with the ball. In this way, Topspin creates a kind of safety for the player, permitting him to exert maximum power and control. This gives the player a greater sense of confidence. Players also use rotation to create force. Why is Topspin so invaluable? Most of today's pro players hit between 2,700 to 3,000 plus RPMs on the forehand of the stroke, depending on the playing surface. In today's modern game, creating maximum power through force and velocity does not depend on how close to the top the ball clears the net, but on the amount of rotation used to keep it in the court. All things combined, Topspin creates more emergencies for the opponent's game and lack of prediction in his ability to develop each point. Although tennis commentators habitually use the term flat shot, in reality ball rotation above 2,000 RPMs is very common whether on serves or ground strokes. In essence, learning Topspin from the beginning of a player's career, mindful of how well

he finds the ball, promotes safety and confidence so that the harder he hits the ball, the more he goes in and the more successfully he is able to play. How Topspin affects time? Brushing the racket up and across creates a longer sensation of feel than a flat stroke. Although actual contact is increased by only milliseconds, this increased feel adds another dimension to the game, the change in the perception of time. Some may argue that brushing up on the ball creates a weak shot. To the contrary, when combining a heightened sensation of feel of the ball on the strings with a brushing motion, the player can create maximum spin and power all the while keeping the ball in the court. The mental calculation of time by thinking is replaced with direct perception through feel, quieting the mind substantially and giving the player a sense of expanded time and greater control. Rotation. Rotation is the action of a body turning on its own axis. In tennis, players use rotation to create power. Along with changes in racket and string technology, MTMs increased use of ball rotation contributed greatly to a revolution in tennis technique and became a major actor in defining so-called modern tennis. Stop athletes seek to achieve a sense of ease and comfort to conserve energy, maximize power and maintain endurance. This suggests that exertion should be produced efficiently, that is, using the minimum amount

of force to produce the maximum result. It is usually to try an error that the player discovers how nature acts to assist rather than oppose his athletic effort. The MTM secret. The simple way to create force in tennis, shorten the radius of the stroke and suddenly change the direction of effort, the direction in which the racket is moving. Per Newton's second law, pulling the racket up, across and back, creates ball rotation and causes the racket to accelerate, permitting its mass to assist its speed and thereby the speed of the ball. The greater the pull of the hand upward, across and back, the more acceleration is achieved by the head of the racket. The sudden change of speed and direction of the racket head creates maximum acceleration with minimum force applied. This pull actually occurs milliseconds before impact, so that natural, rather than forced effort ensues. This is a secret of how MTM creates more power with less effort and optimal results. Action and reaction. The most powerful action in nature is affinity, the attraction or compatibility between particles, elements, structures or things. In order for particles not to collapse into each other through such attraction, a reaction of counter-force is necessary. This phenomenon is expressed in Newton's third law of motion. For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. This is accomplished with rotation. Affinity is a defining element in an individual particle, and the pull of gravity within itself

in ease of execution. Roll of the hand. In modern tennis, the hand leads the action of the body in finding the ball and executing the ideal stroke. Although it is true that the kinetic chain starts from the ground up, the player's attention is mainly on the hand. The movement of the body adjusts intuitively to the needs of the hand. Ideal contact point for top thing. Although the industry standard recommendation for contact is at or surrounding the center point of the string bed, the so-called sweet spot, the ideal point of contact for top thing ground strokes is the area closer to the bottom portion of the strings near the frame. In contact here keeps the angle of the racket face closed. Closing the racket face aids in creating top thing by mitigating the upward pull of the racket and creating increased ball rotation. As I recommend in my landmark ESPN International Tips, it is often thought that center hits the key to the game, but the top pros don't do that. On the bottom of the racket for top thing, on the top of the racket for slice, you don't have to tighten up on the hand and you get a lot more feel. On the top thing forehand, bottom of the racket. On the slice, top of the racket. That's the way to play. Acceleration versus momentum. Acceleration is here defined as an increase in an object's rate of speed. It is created by an unbalanced force acting on an object, Newton's second law of motion.

Force equals mass times acceleration. Momentum is defined as a quantity of motion of a moving body. It is created by the product of the object's mass and velocity. Momentum equals mass times velocity. Angular momentum describes the momentum of an object moving in a circular path, while linear momentum measures an object's motion in a straight line. Linear versus rotational movement. Rotation is more easily produced by the body rotating around its own axis than by moving forward in a linear direction. All things being equal, the effect of acceleration is much more powerful than the effect of momentum. This is why rotation is superior to linear force. Speed accelerates dramatically just before impact. Slows due to the impact of the incoming ball, then speeds up again as it moves towards the finish of the stroke. Conversely, linear movement of the racket causes it to decelerate when players turn sideways to engage the body in forward motion. Power is generated by their weight and momentum, but at the cost. Rapid recovery and ease of motion may be compromised and require compensatory moves, such as twirling, jumping, or taking an extra step from a closed into an open stance. Source of power, contrary to popular belief, the most efficient source of power in tennis is not from the take back to the point of contact, POC. In the modern game, power is generated from close to the point of contact across to the

finish. The racket actually moves slowly in the initial phase of the stroke. It accelerates just before contact loses speed due to impact with incoming ball, then increases speed from pulling up, across, and back toward the finish as the body rotates, as shown in the following photos, Feather and Serena exert force of the racket against the ball with intention of accelerating the racket toward the finish of the stroke, as Zarenka, in contrast, uses force through the contact zone, decelerating her hand in the racket. Summary Circular motion is a fundamental motion in the physical universe. Introduction of greater rotational forces revolutionized tennis. In tennis, players use rotation to create power. Acceleration is more easily produced by rotational rather than by forward linear effort. Rotation facilitates more efficient chord coverage. Power is from the point of contact to finish, not from take back to point of contact. Tossing creates safety and confidence in the player. Tossing challenges the opponent and makes prediction more difficult. Tossing is ideally taught from the beginning and further developed throughout the player's training. Use of heavy topspin as a mainstay of modern tennis continues to evolve the game.
